summary: This Wikipedia-derived note surveys Southeast Asia across religion, history, arts, geography and environment. It covers the spread of Islam through trade, Sufi missionaries and ruling classes, the diversity of Buddhism, Christianity, Hinduism and local beliefs, and the region's Hindu-influenced arts such as wayang kulit and Khmer dance. It also summarizes the region's population, climate, overseas Chinese business networks, and environmental problems like deforestation and haze.
one_line: Overview of Southeast Asia's religions, Islamisation, Hindu-influenced arts, geography, population, climate, overseas Chinese economy and haze pollution.
key_facts: Islam is the most widely practised religion in Southeast Asia, with approximately 240 million adherents, about 40% of the population.
Buddhism is predominant in Thailand, Cambodia, Laos, Burma, Vietnam and Singapore.
The Philippines has the largest Roman Catholic population in Asia.
The Sultanate of Kedah was established in year 1136 after King Phra Ong Mahawangsa converted to Islam.
Samudera Pasai converted to Islam in the year 1267.
The ruler of the Malacca Sultanate embraced Islam in the 15th century, heralding accelerated conversion across the region.
The wayang kulit (shadow puppet) show was recognized by UNESCO on November 7, 2003, as a Masterpiece of Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.
As of 2013, around 625 million people lived in Southeast Asia, and Java, with 143 million people, is the most densely populated large island in the world.
Indonesia had 255 million people as of 2015 and was the 4th most populous country in the world.
Some 30 million overseas Chinese live in Southeast Asia.
Hamka (1908–1981) wrote in 1961: "The development of Islam in Indonesia and Malaya is intimately related to a Chinese Muslim, Admiral Zheng He."
All Southeast Asian states except East Timor are members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
The two worst regional hazes were in 1997 and 2006, mostly caused by "slash and burn" activities in Sumatra and Borneo.
Predictions have been made that more than 40% of the animal and plant species in Southeast Asia could be wiped out in the 21st century.
The bamboo network is a network of overseas Chinese businesses operating in Southeast Asian markets that share common family and cultural ties.
